items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: that's when I first met Ben Webster and Hot Lips Page, you know.

ctx.x: a basketball player or a baseball player. I loved the sports. But to see the football games, I began to play in the band because we could get in and see the football games free, you know. So I joined the band just to see the football games. And I was getting around 14, there.

I met Sy -- Louie Armstrong was coming through Columbus at the time, all the time. And I would sneak in to hear him. And at that time they had all the big bands coming through Columbus. It was a big dance town because they had fantastic dance hall called Valley Dale, which the blacks couldn't go to but you could stand on the outside of the fence and hear the bands play, you see. Like Benny Moten would come through there and that's when I first met Ben Webster and Hot Lips Page, you know. Because I was living next…

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Like Hot Lips Page used to do, he could take a note and do more with it than the average trumpet player take a thousand notes

ctx.x: Sinatra record, it could be on a sound track, it could be on a jazz recording and you know immediately it’s you.

I’ve tried to be original and as I said before, everybody in my era, they were identifiable. Nobody sounds like Benny Carter, he’s got a sound of his own. Nobody sounded like Chu Berry, nobody sounded like Art Tatum. Nobody sounded alike in that era, period. You can’t name anybody that sounded alike in that era that I was coming up. So, I was just following a trend, I was just trying to be original myself, trying to play the only way I knew how and that was, like Basie used to say, “If you don’t know the chords…
Could you say that Basie’s piano actually had some effect on your developing this trumpet style.
